title: Right or Reachable
summary: Tallyho keeps group travel wallets in two regions. When the ocean link drops, every request has to pick: the right answer, or an answer at all.

goals.text: See what a network partition forces you to choose
Compare refusing writes with accepting and diverging
Choose consistency per kind of data
Use quorums (R + W > N) to tune reads and writes
Trade latency for consistency even without failures

steps.title: One wallet, two continents
body: Tallyho runs shared travel wallets: a group tops up €100 and anyone can spend from it. To keep the app fast for everyone, the data lives in Frankfurt and in Virginia.
Every write is copied to the other region before it's confirmed — synchronous replication. Both copies always agree, at the price of an ocean round trip on every write.

steps.title: The ocean link drops
body: A transatlantic route fails. Both regions are healthy and serving users, but they can't talk to each other: a network partition.

Every write now hangs, waiting for a confirmation that will never come. The CAP theorem says this moment is a forced choice: while partitioned, a replicated system can stay consistent or stay available — not both.

callout.text: Partitions aren't optional. Cables get cut and switches fail; the only question is what your system does when it happens.

changes: ~ Writes stuck waiting for the other side

card.title: CAP, during a partition
lines: **C**onsistent: every read sees the latest write
**A**vailable: every request gets a real answer
! with the link down you can't promise both

steps.title: Option 1: stay correct
body: A CP system refuses what it can't make safe. Writes that can't reach the other region fail fast with an error; reads still work but may be a few minutes old.
Nobody overdraws the wallet — and nobody can pay for dinner either. For the length of the outage, Tallyho is partly down on both continents.
changes: ~ Reads still served from the local copy

steps.title: Option 2: stay reachable
body: An AP system keeps accepting writes on both sides and promises to reconcile later. Everything feels normal: payments go through in 25 ms in each region.
But the two copies are now quietly telling different stories. Frankfurt thinks the wallet holds €40, Virginia thinks €30, and each is approving new spending against its own number.

steps.title: The link comes back
body: When the partition heals, each region ships its backlog to the other — and they disagree. Two payments were each approved against €100, together spending €130.
Someone must reconcile. Last-write-wins keeps one version and silently drops the other expense. For money, neither answer is acceptable after the fact.

callout.text: AP doesn't remove conflicts — it postpones them until after the partition, when they're harder to undo.

card.title: Same wallet, two histories
lines: # last-write-wins would silently drop one expense

steps.title: Choose per kind of data
body: The choice isn't per system, it's per operation. Wallet spending gets a home region (Virginia): during a partition, Frankfurt refuses spending rather than guess. That's CP where it matters.
Comments and reactions are AP: accept them everywhere and merge later. A set of comments merges cleanly — keep everything from both sides — so there's nothing to lose by staying available.

callout.text: Data that merges naturally (sets, counters, append-only logs) is a great fit for AP. Data with invariants (balances, stock, seats) usually isn't.

changes: ~ Wallet writes routed to a single home region
~ Comments accepted in both regions and merged

steps.title: Quorums: overlap by arithmetic
body: Inside a region, stores like Cassandra or DynamoDB keep N copies of each row and let you choose how many must answer. A write waits for W replicas; a read asks R replicas and takes the newest version.
If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica — so a read always sees the latest confirmed write, even while replica 3 is still catching up.

card.title: Quorum arithmetic
lines: = R + W = 4 > 3 → every read meets the latest write

steps.title: Lose a replica, keep going
body: Replica 1 dies. With R = 2 and W = 2, the remaining two still form a quorum for both reads and writes — nobody notices.

R and W are dials: lower them for speed and availability, raise them for stronger reads. Eventual consistency (R = 1, W = 1) is fastest, but a read may land on a replica that hasn't heard the latest write yet.
changes: ~ Reads and writes use replicas 2 and 3

card.title: Turning the dials (N = 3)
lines: R=1 W=1 · fastest · reads may be stale
R=2 W=2 · overlap · survives 1 replica down
R=1 W=3 · cheap reads · 1 replica down blocks writes
! lose 2 replicas and R=2 / W=2 can't be met

steps.title: Even without failures
body: Partitions are rare; latency is every request. PACELC extends CAP: if Partitioned, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
Comments now commit locally in 25 ms and replicate asynchronously, about 300 ms behind. To hide the lag from the author, read their own data from the region they wrote to — read-your-writes.
changes: ~ Writes commit in the local region

card.title: Else: latency or consistency
lines: # p95 of a wallet write, no partition

steps.title: Right, reachable, or fast
body:
• During a partition you choose: refuse (consistent) or accept and reconcile later (available).
  • Make the choice per kind of data — money CP, comments AP.
  • Quorums with R + W > N give consistent reads while tolerating failed replicas.
  • Without failures, the trade is latency versus consistency.
